title: Minimum Sum of Squared Difference
statement:
Two arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of the same length `n` hold non-negative integers. Their *squared difference* is the total of `(nums1[i] - nums2[i])^2` taken over every index `i`.

A move adds 1 to, or subtracts 1 from, one element. You may spend at most `k1` moves on elements of `nums1` and at most `k2` moves on elements of `nums2`; the same element can be moved many times, and values may become negative. Return the smallest squared difference you can reach.
signature: long minSumSquareDiff(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k1, int k2)
notes:
## Intuition

Only the gap `|nums1[i] - nums2[i]|` at each index matters, and a move on either array can shrink one gap by 1, so `k1` and `k2` are really one budget of `k1 + k2` moves. Shrinking a gap `g` to `g - 1` saves `2g - 1`, which is largest for the largest gap. The brute force spends moves one at a time on the current largest gap; the fast version does the same thing in bulk by lowering the tallest gaps together, like draining the top of a bar chart.

## Approach

1. Build `diffs`, sort it from largest to smallest and append a `0` as a floor.
2. Keep the first `width` gaps flattened to the same `level`. Bringing that group down to the next gap `diffs[width]` costs `(level - diffs[width]) * width`.
3. While the budget `moves` covers that `cost`, pay it, drop `level` and widen the group.
4. If the group reached the floor, every gap is 0 and the answer is 0.
5. Otherwise spread the remaining moves evenly: every member drops `floor(moves / width)` and `moves % width` of them (`lowered`) drop one more.
6. Add the squares of the group and of the untouched gaps after it.

## Example 1, step by step

No moves are allowed (`k1 = k2 = 0`). Sorted `diffs` is `[17, 15, 8, 1, 0]`. Lowering `17` to `15` costs 2, more than 0, so the loop stops with `level = 17`, `width = 1`, `lowered = 0`. The total is `17² + 15² + 8² + 1² = 289 + 225 + 64 + 1 = 579`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): sorting dominates, and the loop and final sum are linear.
- Space: O(n) for `diffs`.

## Pitfalls

- Moving `nums1[i]` up is the same as moving `nums2[i]` down, so do not budget the two arrays separately.
- `k1 + k2` can exceed the total gap; stop at 0 instead of letting `level` go negative.
- After the loop the leftover moves are fewer than one full step, so split them as `floor` and remainder instead of lowering the whole group again.
- Answers reach about 10^15 on LeetCode's limits, so Java and C need a 64-bit total.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `diffs` | gaps sorted from largest to smallest, ending with a 0 floor |
| `moves` | budget still unspent |
| `level` | common value of the flattened top group |
| `width` | number of gaps in that group |
| `cost` | moves needed to lower the group to the next gap |
| `lowered` | members that drop one extra step |
| `total` | sum of squared gaps at the end |

narration.3: Sort the gaps from largest to smallest so the tallest ones come first.
narration.4: Append a 0 floor so the group can always be lowered one more step, all the way to zero.
narration.5: A move on either array shrinks one gap by 1, so the two budgets merge into one.

narration.25: Gaps below the group were never touched; add their squares as they are.
narration.28: Return the smallest possible sum of squared differences.
